findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Update parent epic e369's Approach step 5 to replace the `docker run -dit -p 2990:2990 pycontribs/jira-test-image:8.17.1` instruction with the verified build-from-vendored-Dockerfile approach (vendored `tests/live_jira_dc/Dockerfile` FROM addono base by digest), re-staling the parent's plan-review attestation and triggering re-review before J5's containment is clean.
evidence: Parent e369 step 5: 'the oracle is the pinned image `pycontribs/jira-test-image:8.17.1`, run as `docker run -dit -p 2990:2990 pycontribs/jira-test-image:8.17.1`'

J5 Approach: 'The image must be BUILT, not pulled — corrected against the registry, not assumed. An earlier draft of this plan said to `docker run pycontribs/jira-test-image:8.17.1` and called it "a pinned, pullable image". That is false'
J5 AC 1: 'The criterion is explicitly BUILD-and-start, not pull-and-start: no acceptance step may depend on `pycontribs/jira-test-image` being pullable, because it is not published'
findings.finding: J5 redefines the image acquisition mechanism in a way that directly contradicts the parent's explicit instruction. The parent (e369, Approach step 5) specifies `docker run -dit -p 2990:2990 pycontribs/jira-test-image:8.17.1` — a pull-and-run model — as the harness substrate. J5 explicitly states this formulation is 'false' and instead delivers a build-from-vendored-Dockerfile mechanism using the addono base image. Even though J5's factual correction is sound, under G7 the parent wins on any conflict; a leaf may not silently redefine a parent deliverable. The parent's plan must be updated first to replace the `docker run pycontribs/jira-test-image:8.17.1` instruction with the verified build-from-Dockerfile approach, staling the parent's plan-review attestation and requiring re-review, before J5 can be treated as a pure subset.
findings.location: Parent e369 Approach step 5 (`docker run -dit -p 2990:2990 pycontribs/jira-test-image:8.17.1`) vs J5 Approach section ('The image must be BUILT, not pulled') and J5 AC 1 ('The criterion is explicitly BUILD-and-start, not pull-and-start')
scenarios: A reviewer validating J5 against the parent finds the parent says 'docker run' (pull from registry) while J5 says 'docker build' (build from vendored Dockerfile) — this is a direct contradiction, not a narrowing.
The parent's plan-review attestation was certified against the old (pull-based) description of J5's approach; J5 has since changed the mechanism without the parent being updated.
findings.suggested_fix: In e369 Approach step 5, replace: 'the oracle is the pinned image `pycontribs/jira-test-image:8.17.1`, run as `docker run -dit -p 2990:2990 pycontribs/jira-test-image:8.17.1`' with: 'the oracle is built from a vendored `tests/live_jira_dc/Dockerfile` that FROM's the addono/jira-software-standalone base by digest (the `pycontribs/jira-test-image` tag is a local-build name, not a published registry image — verified false before J5 was written); the compose file builds locally and the harness is started via `make jira-dc-up`'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify a concrete default readiness-probe timeout and poll interval in the plan (e.g., 10-minute max, 15-second poll), document the env-var name (`JIRA_READY_TIMEOUT`), and ensure the probe exits with a non-zero code and a clear message after the deadline — so slow runners get a tunable knob and stuck instances don't hang CI.
evidence: Plan: 'the readiness probe's timeout is generous and overridable by env var rather than a hardcoded few minutes'
No default value (e.g., '10 minutes') or retry interval (e.g., 'poll every 10 s') is given anywhere in the plan.
The failure path AC says the probe emits a clear message when the instance is down, but only specifies the message content, not the timeout after which that message is emitted.
findings.finding: The readiness probe is described as polling 'until the instance answers REST' with a timeout that is 'generous and overridable by env var', but no default maximum poll duration or retry cadence is specified. If the Jira instance fails to start silently (e.g., Maven resolution fails inside the container without exiting, or the `-DskipAllPrompts` flag is inadvertently dropped), the probe could hang indefinitely or time out too aggressively depending on the unspecified default.
findings.location: Approach — readiness probe paragraph; AC line: 'readiness timeout is env-overridable'
scenarios: On a slow CI runner or under heavy load, the default timeout (unspecified) proves too short; the probe fires 'harness not running' on a valid but slow startup, causing false-negative test failures.
The container starts but Jira's webapp never becomes responsive (OOM, Maven hang); with no specified maximum wait the probe loops forever and blocks the CI job.
findings.suggested_fix: In `conftest.py` use `timeout = int(os.environ.get('JIRA_READY_TIMEOUT', '600'))` (600 s = 10 min) with a 15-second sleep between polls; after exhausting the timeout, raise `pytest.skip` or a named exception with the message 'Jira DC harness did not become ready within {timeout}s — is jira-dc-up running?'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify in the `jira-dc-up` Makefile target (or in the fixture's session-scoped setup) whether the container is always recreated from scratch (e.g., `docker-compose down -v && docker-compose up`), OR require the fixture to use a unique project key per session (e.g., timestamp/UUID suffix) so stale state from a prior run cannot collide with a new run.
evidence: Plan scope: 'a `jira-dc-up` target only' — no mention of `--force-recreate`, volume removal, or fresh-state guarantee.
Teardown oracle only covers the current session's issues ('every issue the fixture created returns 404'); it does not address state inherited from a prior incomplete teardown.
Jira stores its data inside the container; if the container is not recreated, that data persists.
findings.finding: The plan does not specify whether `jira-dc-up` forces a fresh container (e.g., `docker-compose up --force-recreate` or a volume wipe), so if a previous run left the container running with an interrupted teardown, the next run inherits stale Jira state — leftover projects and issues that the fixture's CREATE step may collide with or that pollute assertions.
findings.location: Scope — `Makefile` `jira-dc-up` target; Testing — teardown oracle
scenarios: A test run is SIGKILL'd mid-teardown; container stays up with orphaned issues. Next `pytest` invocation finds unexpected issues/projects, causing assertion failures unrelated to the code under test.
A developer iterates on a test, runs it twice without restarting the container; the second run creates a duplicate project key and Jira returns a 400, masking the real behavior under test.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `docker-compose down -v` before `docker-compose up -d --build` in the `jira-dc-up` target to guarantee a clean Jira data directory on each invocation; document this in README as the intended lifecycle.

Plan nowhere declares the intended network access class for this service (e.g. 'loopback-only, ephemeral CI use only')
findings.finding: The compose service publishes `2990:2990` without restricting the bind address to the loopback interface, exposing the ephemeral admin/admin Jira instance on all host network interfaces. The plan does not declare this port's access posture (loopback-only / ephemeral-test-only / intentionally open on LAN), which is itself the gap per the undeclared-access-posture framing.
findings.location: Scope section / `tests/live_jira_dc/docker-compose.yml` / AC line: "publishes `2990:2990`"
scenarios: On a shared CI runner or developer's LAN, any peer on the same subnet can reach the unauthenticated Jira admin interface during the test run.
A multi-tenant CI environment (e.g. GitHub Actions self-hosted runner pool) could have another job or host scanning open ports and reaching the admin panel.
findings.suggested_fix: In `docker-compose.yml`, change the port mapping to `127.0.0.1:2990:2990` to restrict the bind to loopback only. If a non-loopback bind is needed for some CI topology, add a comment in both the compose file and README declaring the access class as "ephemeral-test-only, no production data, acceptable on trusted CI networks" so the posture is explicit.

findings.location: Approach section — teardown oracle paragraph; Testing section — 'teardown oracle' bullet; Acceptance Criteria AC5
scenarios: A second, slightly different teardown implementation drifts from ADR 0037's 'leak-loud' guarantee (e.g., missing the backoff or the CI artifact log) — a stray issue silently pollutes the local Jira instance.
A future story wants to add bilateral (local-id) teardown to this harness and discovers the pattern was rebuilt rather than extracted, forcing a third implementation.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a `conftest.py` in `tests/live_jira_dc/` that auto-applies `pytest.mark.integration` to every item in the directory (mirroring how `tests/conftest.py` auto-applies `external` to `tests/external/`), or document in the README and AC that the marker must be manually applied to every new test file added to that directory.
evidence: tests/conftest.py::pytest_collection_modifyitems auto-applies `external` to all items under tests/external/ and hard-fails if an `external`-marked test escapes that directory — no analogous guard exists for `integration`
tests/unit/test_external_isolation.py::test_no_external_marked_test_outside_external_dir provides a durable AST-scan confinement test for `external`; no equivalent exists for `integration`
Plan text: 'Every test in the directory carries the existing integration marker' — stated as authoring discipline, not structural enforcement
AC #6: 'pytest --collect-only -m "not integration and not external" reports 0 tests collected from tests/live_jira_dc/' — verifies current state at implementation time only
findings.finding: The `integration`-marker exclusion mechanism has no structural backstop: unlike the `external` tier (which has both conftest auto-injection in `tests/conftest.py::pytest_collection_modifyitems` AND the `test_no_external_marked_test_outside_external_dir` confinement guard), the `integration` marker on `tests/live_jira_dc/` tests relies entirely on per-file manual declaration. If a future contributor adds a test file to `tests/live_jira_dc/` without the marker, it will silently leak into `make test`'s default `-m 'not integration and not external'` run, because nothing auto-applies or enforces the marker for that directory. The gating AC (#6) snapshots the state at implementation time but does not create a durable invariant.
findings.location: Scope / Testing / AC #6 — 'Every test in the directory carries the existing `integration` marker'
scenarios: A contributor adds tests/live_jira_dc/test_new_scenario.py without pytestmark = pytest.mark.integration — it immediately runs in make test, potentially failing the CI default suite when Docker is not running

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Cite the Atlassian release note or Server changelog entry confirming that Jira 8.14 (Server/DC) introduced Personal Access Tokens, and add that citation as a comment in the Dockerfile or README so maintainers can verify the version boundary when bumping `JIRA_VERSION`.
evidence: Plan states: 'Jira 8.17.1 is **≥ 8.14**, the release that introduced Personal Access Tokens, so the PAT bearer auth the DC transport uses is exercised for real.'
No Atlassian release note, Jira changelog URL, or other source is cited for this version boundary.
This claim directly gates AC item 4: 'a PAT-authenticated request succeeds' — if the version boundary is wrong, the test proves nothing meaningful about PAT auth.
findings.finding: The plan asserts 'Jira 8.14 introduced Personal Access Tokens' as the basis for the auth AC ('PAT bearer auth the DC transport uses is exercised for real'), but cites no Atlassian release note, changelog, or documentation for this version boundary. If the actual PAT introduction version differs, the auth test path and the README constraint both need revision.
findings.location: Approach section, paragraph 2: 'Jira 8.17.1 is ≥ 8.14, the release that introduced Personal Access Tokens'
scenarios: A maintainer bumping JIRA_VERSION within 8.x to a pre-8.14 patch version would silently break PAT auth with no warning.
If PATs were actually introduced in a different release (e.g., 8.20 or a Server-only backport), the test runs on a version that doesn't support them and the bearer auth AC is vacuous.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a comment in `tests/live_jira_dc/README.md` such as: 'PATs were introduced in Jira 8.14 (Server/DC) — see https://confluence.atlassian.com/enterprise/using-personal-access-tokens-1026032365.html — so any 8.14+ image exercises real bearer auth.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a traceable source for the 9+/11+ Maven resolution failure constraint (e.g., a link to the pycontribs `docker/jira-test-image/README.md`, a specific Maven error, or the addono image's own documentation) so the README's warning is verifiable and can be re-evaluated if the upstream image changes.
evidence: Plan states: 'JIRA_VERSION is overridable across 8.x patch versions, but 9+/11+ fail Maven resolution because the upstream pom is anchored to the 8.x dependency graph.'
No link to the addono Dockerfile/README, the pycontribs docker/jira-test-image/README.md, a Maven build log, or any upstream issue is provided.

The README AC requires this constraint be documented: 'states … that only Jira 8.x works on this base (9+/11+ fail Maven resolution)' — but if the rationale is wrong, the README will propagate a false claim.
findings.finding: The plan asserts that Jira versions 9+/11+ 'fail Maven resolution because the upstream pom is anchored to the 8.x dependency graph' as a hard constraint requiring README documentation, but cites no upstream source (addono README, pycontribs README, Maven error log, or test result) for this claim. Without a source, a future maintainer who sees the constraint has no way to verify it or determine whether it has been fixed upstream.
findings.location: Approach section, detail 3: 'Only Jira 8.x is supported … 9+/11+ fail Maven resolution because the upstream pom is anchored to the 8.x dependency graph'
scenarios: A maintainer reading the README tries to upgrade to 9.x for a client on Jira 9 and gets a confusing Maven error with no pointer to the root cause.
If the upstream image or AMPS plugin was later updated to support 9.x, the constraint silently holds back an unnecessary restriction with no way to re-evaluate it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Record the addono base image feasibility proof as a reproducible artifact (e.g., a `docker manifest inspect` snippet in the README confirming the digest resolves, or a CI run link) and add a contingency note for what to do if the digest becomes unavailable.
evidence: Plan states feasibility was 'proven' but does not cite a CI run, a commit, a log file, or a specific host environment.
The addono digest `sha256:04326628dc4ac36b2bfc1d0f2ebe5ba3807c1ec9cf9b18307d3c2ad7222537e9` is cited as 'resolves' — but no Docker Hub manifest URL or `docker manifest inspect` output is linked.
ABSENCE: no `tests/live_jira_dc/` directory exists in the repo yet, so there is no committed Dockerfile to inspect.
findings.finding: The plan claims feasibility was 'proven before this rewrite' (879 MB image, container starts and stays up) but provides no reproducible artifact — no CI log URL, no commit SHA, no recorded container health-check output. If the proof was done on a specific host or Docker version that is no longer available, the feasibility claim cannot be independently validated by a reviewer or reproduced in CI.
findings.location: Approach section: 'Feasibility was proven before this rewrite: the upstream Dockerfile was fetched and built on the target host (879 MB image, container starts and stays up).'
scenarios: The addono base image digest becomes unavailable (registry purge, account deletion) between the feasibility test and implementation — the plan has no fallback.
A reviewer or CI system on a different Docker daemon version cannot reproduce the startup behavior and cannot tell whether the 'proven' result generalizes.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Restrict the compose port binding to loopback (`127.0.0.1:2990:2990` instead of `2990:2990`) OR add an explicit, justified rationale in the README and compose file explaining why non-loopback exposure is acceptable given the admin/admin credentials (e.g., single-tenant CI network, ephemeral runner).
evidence: Plan states compose 'publishes 2990:2990' without specifying interface binding
Plan states default credentials are admin/admin (well-known, no rotation)

T10-b2 requires: for every network-reachable service stood up, the plan states how HUMAN principals authenticate OR provides an explicit justified no-auth rationale (loopback-only / behind authenticating gateway / single-tenant private network) — none of these rationales is stated
findings.finding: The compose file publishes `2990:2990`, which in Docker binds to all network interfaces (0.0.0.0) by default, not just loopback. Combined with the well-known default credentials (`admin`/`admin`), the Jira admin UI and REST API are reachable from any host on the same network with full administrative access. The plan neither restricts the binding to `127.0.0.1:2990:2990` nor provides an explicit rationale for why non-loopback exposure is acceptable (e.g., CI runner is single-tenant / isolated network).
findings.location: Scope section — `docker-compose.yml` description: 'publishes 2990:2990'; AC line: 'sets platform: linux/amd64 … and publishes 2990:2990'
scenarios: Developer running the harness on a laptop connected to a shared office or home network inadvertently exposes a Jira admin console with admin/admin credentials to other network participants
CI runner with a shared or multi-tenant network exposes the instance during the test window
findings.suggested_fix: In `docker-compose.yml`, change the ports stanza to `- "127.0.0.1:2990:2990"`. This makes the loopback-only intent explicit and machine-enforced rather than assumed. Add a one-line comment: `# loopback-only: admin/admin credentials; not safe to expose on a shared network`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify whether the harness is intended to verify REST v2 (which matches `probe.py`) or REST v3 (which matches the bulk of the DC adapter); if v3, confirm that `/rest/api/3/` endpoints including `POST /rest/api/3/search/jql` are available on Jira 8.17.1 Server/DC and update AC4 and the smoke test to exercise the v3 surface the adapter actually uses.
evidence: Plan states: 'this harness proves REST v2 protocol semantics'
acli_rest.py, acli_graph.py, acli.py use /rest/api/3/issue/, /rest/api/3/search/jql, /rest/api/3/user/assignable/search throughout
Only probe.py (/rest/api/2/issue/{key}) and get_myself (/rest/api/2/myself) use v2
AC1: 'REST v2 answering at http://localhost:2990/jira' — readiness probe tests v2 availability, not v3
AC4: 'creates and reads back an issue via REST v2' — smoke test exercises v2 while adapter uses v3
Jira 8.x Server/DC does expose both /rest/api/2/ and /rest/api/3/ — but the plan never asserts this and never verifies /rest/api/3/ is available on 8.17.1
Evidence class: Partially-verified (v2 is confirmed via probe.py usage; v3 availability on 8.17.1 Server is Unverified)
findings.finding: The plan specifies the smoke test 'creates and reads back an issue via REST v2' and the teardown oracle polls '/rest/api/2/issue/{key}', but the actual DC adapter code uses /rest/api/3/ for all primary operations (issue CRUD, transitions, labels, comments, assignee resolution, JQL search). Jira 8.x Server/DC supports both v2 and v3 at the same base URL, but the plan's stated purpose is to prove the REST surface the DC transport uses — and that surface is v3, not v2. Whether /rest/api/3/ is fully available on Jira 8.17.1 Server is unverified by the plan.
findings.location: Approach section ('REST v2 protocol semantics'), Testing section ('creates and reads back one issue through raw REST v2'), AC item 1 ('REST v2 answering'), AC item 4 ('creates and reads back an issue via REST v2'), AC item 5 ('direct issue endpoint')
scenarios: The smoke test passes on v2 but the adapter silently fails on v3 if /rest/api/3/ behaves differently or is absent on 8.17.1 Server — the harness would give false confidence.
A future maintainer reading 'proves REST v2 protocol semantics' and the v2-only smoke test would not know to test the v3 endpoints the adapter actually calls.
If Jira 8.17.1 Server does not support POST /rest/api/3/search/jql (introduced later or Cloud-only), the adapter's JQL search path breaks silently while the harness passes.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a PAT lifecycle note to the plan (and implement in `conftest.py`): the minted PAT should be revoked via the Jira REST API in the fixture's teardown, and the test should mask the token value from pytest's captured output (e.g. via `capfd`/monkeypatching or by never printing it) so it does not appear in CI logs.
evidence: Plan states 'a Personal Access Token minted on the 8.17.1 instance authenticates a request via `Authorization: Bearer`'
Teardown section describes polling for 404 on created issues and asserting delete HTTP status — no mention of PAT revocation
Plan does not state whether the PAT value is stored as a pytest fixture variable, logged, or emitted to stdout during the test run
ABSENCE: no secret-lifecycle note for the PAT in any section of the plan
findings.finding: The smoke test mints a Personal Access Token on the live Jira instance to prove PAT bearer auth, but the plan does not declare how that PAT is stored during the test run, whether it appears in captured pytest output or CI logs, or whether the fixture revokes it on teardown. The teardown description covers project/issue cleanup but is silent on PAT lifecycle.
findings.location: Testing section (auth path) / `tests/live_jira_dc/conftest.py` teardown description / AC line: "a PAT-authenticated request succeeds"
scenarios: If pytest's default output or CI log capture records the Bearer token value, the PAT leaks into CI logs for the lifetime of the instance (which, though ephemeral, could be retrieved if logs are persisted).
A future maintainer adds a longer-lived harness container (e.g. for iterative local development) without realising the PAT from a prior run was never revoked and still appears in logs.
findings.suggested_fix: In `conftest.py`, after the PAT-authenticated assertion, call `DELETE /rest/pat/latest/tokens/{tokenId}` (the Jira 8.x PAT revocation endpoint) in the fixture's teardown block. Also pass the raw token through a helper that masks it in logs rather than asserting on its string value directly.
